    Going Further

    Last updated on 2026-11-24 | Edit this page

    The lesson teaches one way to do each task. This page lists what comes next: other methods, bigger models and the theory the lesson leaves out. Each paragraph names the episode it extends. None of it is needed for the capstone.

    Topics Beyond This Lesson

    Profile-likelihood intervals for standard deviations. Extends Random Effects and Many Stocks. ci_table() builds every interval from a standard error, which works poorly for a standard deviation (SD) close to zero. A profile interval instead refits the model with the parameter held at a range of values and keeps the values the data support. TMB::tmbprofile() computes it, and both episodes show it in an optional box. For an SD estimated at zero the profile is flat and its interval is unreliable too: report the estimate and the comparison by Akaike information criterion (AIC) instead.

    REML for variance components. Extends Many Stocks. Standard deviations of random effects estimated by maximum likelihood are a little too small. Listing the overall mean in random = as well, random = c("log_alpha_stock", "mean_log_alpha") (restricted maximum likelihood, REML), gives a less biased SD. For Episode 10’s stock model, the between-stock SD rises from 0.106 to 0.127. Use REML to report SDs, not to compare models: AIC needs the ordinary fits.

    Heavier tails for extreme years. Extends Residuals and Simulation. Stellako’s brood year 2005 is far below every other year, and a normal distribution finds it very surprising. A Student-t distribution, RTMB’s dt(), expects an occasional extreme year. For Stellako, a random walk with Student-t yearly scatter lowers AIC from 178.3 to 170.9.

    Year effects correlated from year to year. Extends Random Effects and Many Stocks. The shared year effects of Episode 10 are independent of each other. RTMB’s dautoreg() lets neighbouring years be alike, between independent years and a random walk. Another extension gives every stock its own random walk in productivity.

    Cycles and the Larkin model. Extends Comparing Models. Some Fraser stocks, such as Quesnel, have strong four-year cycles: a large brood year is followed by smaller ones. The Larkin model adds the spawners of the three previous brood years to the Ricker model. It drops the first three years, so every model it is compared with must be refitted to the same rows. Put spawners in millions to avoid false alarms in the flat check. Challenge 1 below fits it to Chilko.

    map and REPORT(). Extends Fitting and Checking and Comparing Models. map holds a parameter at its starting value without writing a new function; Episode 9 shows it in an optional box. REPORT() returns any value computed inside the function, without a standard error. Read reported values with obj$report(obj$env$last.par.best), never obj$report() alone, which uses whatever parameter values were evaluated last.

    Other forecast scores. Extends Forecasting. The log score rewards a forecast for giving high probability to what happened, and probability integral transform (PIT) plots show whether prediction intervals are too narrow or too wide. Episode 11 shows the log score in an optional box.

    State-space spawner-recruit models. Extends Likelihoods. Spawner counts are measured with error, which biases the regression of log(R/S) on spawners. A state-space model separates the true number of spawners, a random effect, from the measured one.

    Forecasts by return year and age. Extends Forecasting. Real pre-season forecasts predict the adults returning in one calendar year, which come from several brood years (mostly four- and five-year-old fish). The lesson forecasts by brood year instead.

    Bayesian fitting. Extends Fitting and Checking. The tmbstan package on CRAN samples from the same RTMB model objects with Stan, and gives posterior distributions instead of standard errors.

    Formula interfaces for standard models. Extends Many Stocks. When a model is a standard mixed model, a formula package is quicker to write. The glmmTMB package on CRAN gives the same negative log-likelihood (1883.81) for Episode 10’s stock model.

    Custom distributions. Extends Likelihoods. RTMB has the usual R distributions; the RTMBdist package adds more, and you can write your own with support for simulation.

    Documentation and derivations. The RTMB documentation, the TMB documentation and the materials of the original Pacific Salmon Commission RTMB workshop contain the derivations this lesson leaves out: gradients, the Laplace approximation and the delta method.

    Extra Challenges

    These challenges are for fast learners, or for after the workshop. Each starts from this code, run in your project folder:

    R 

    library(RTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
source("files/cookbook.R")
sockeye <- read.csv("data/sockeye.csv")
npgo    <- read.csv("data/npgo.csv")
    Challenge

    Challenge 1 (Optional): A Larkin Model for Chilko (not timed)

    Chilko’s recruits per spawner may also depend on how many spawners there were in the previous few brood years. The Larkin model tests this:

    \[\log(R_t/S_t) = \log\alpha - S_t/S_{max} - b_1 S_{t-1} - b_2 S_{t-2} - b_3 S_{t-3} + \text{noise}\]

    In words: the Ricker model, plus one term for each of the three earlier brood years’ spawners.

    Write nll_larkin, fit it to Chilko, check it, and compare it with the Ricker model using aic_table(). Which brood years affect this year’s productivity?

    • Build the earlier spawners by brood year, not by row: spawners[match(brood_year - 1, brood_year)] inside mutate().
    • The first three brood years have no earlier spawners: drop them, and fit the Ricker model to the same rows.
    • Divide the earlier spawners by 1000 (millions of fish), so that b1 to b3 are not tiny numbers.
    • For mu_new, the earlier spawners of the next brood year are the last three observed ones.

    R 

    chilko <- sockeye %>%
  filter(stock == "Chilko") %>%
  mutate(S1 = spawners[match(brood_year - 1, brood_year)] / 1000,   # millions of fish
         S2 = spawners[match(brood_year - 2, brood_year)] / 1000,
         S3 = spawners[match(brood_year - 3, brood_year)] / 1000) %>%
  filter(!is.na(S3))                                    # drop years without three earlier ones
dat_ch <- make_dat(chilko, S_new = mean(tail(chilko$spawners, 4)))
dat_ch$S1 <- chilko$S1
dat_ch$S2 <- chilko$S2
dat_ch$S3 <- chilko$S3
dat_ch$S_lags_new <- rev(tail(chilko$spawners, 3)) / 1000   # lags 1, 2, 3 for the next year

nll_larkin <- function(par, dat) {
  getAll(par, dat)
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)
  mu     <- log_alpha - S / exp(log_Smax) - b1 * S1 - b2 * S2 - b3 * S3
  mu_new <- log_alpha - S_new / exp(log_Smax) - sum(c(b1, b2, b3) * S_lags_new)
  ADREPORT(mu_new)
  -sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, exp(log_sigma), log = TRUE))
}

larkin_ch <- fit_model(nll_larkin, c(start_ricker(dat_ch), list(b1 = 0, b2 = 0, b3 = 0)), dat_ch)
ricker_ch <- fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat_ch), dat_ch)     # the same 71 rows
larkin_ch$checks
aic_table(list(ricker = ricker_ch, larkin = larkin_ch))
ci_table(larkin_ch)

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE
   model k      AIC checks_ok     dAIC
2 larkin 6 165.3239      TRUE  0.00000
1 ricker 3 185.0405      TRUE 19.71659
  parameter    estimate       lower       upper
1     alpha  18.8998069  13.6324471  26.2023903
2      Smax 535.0998884 324.7446725 881.7138963
3     sigma   0.7123454   0.6043076   0.8396981
4        b1   1.3835859   0.4367815   2.3303903
5        b2   1.3931868   0.4383542   2.3480195
6        b3   0.4090741  -0.5397814   1.3579295

    The Larkin model passes all four checks and is better than the Ricker model by 19.7 AIC units on the same 71 brood years (1951-2021): a decisive difference. Spawners one and two brood years earlier both lower this year’s recruits per spawner: log(R/S) falls by about 1.4 for every million spawners in either year. The interval for three brood years earlier includes zero. b1 to b3 have no log_ prefix because they may be negative, so ci_table() leaves them on their own scale.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2 (Optional): NPGO for Every Stock (not timed)

    Episode 9 found no clear effect of the NPGO index on Stellako. Fit nll_ricker_npgo to each of the 19 stocks separately, and collect the estimate of b_npgo with its 95% confidence interval. How many intervals lie above zero, and how many below? What would you conclude, and what makes you wary?

    Loop over unique(sockeye$stock). Inside the loop, reuse the covariate recipe of Episode 9, and keep the b_npgo row with filter(ci_table(m_s), parameter == "b_npgo").

    R 

    npgo_by_brood <- npgo %>%
  mutate(brood_year = year - 2) %>%
  select(brood_year, npgo)
b_npgo <- NULL
for (s in unique(sockeye$stock)) {
  one   <- filter(sockeye, stock == s) %>% left_join(npgo_by_brood, by = "brood_year")
  dat_s <- make_dat(one, S_new = mean(tail(one$spawners, 4)))
  dat_s$npgo     <- one$npgo
  dat_s$npgo_new <- npgo$npgo[npgo$year == max(one$brood_year) + 3]
  m_s <- fit_model(nll_ricker_npgo, c(start_ricker(dat_s), list(b_npgo = 0)), dat_s)
  b_npgo <- rbind(b_npgo, data.frame(stock = s, filter(ci_table(m_s), parameter == "b_npgo"),
                                     checks_ok = all(m_s$checks)))
}
arrange(b_npgo, estimate)
c(above_zero = sum(b_npgo$lower > 0), below_zero = sum(b_npgo$upper < 0))

    OUTPUT

         5          0

    All 19 fits pass the four checks. Seventeen of the 19 estimates are positive; only Bowron and Early Stuart are negative. Five intervals lie above zero and none lie below: higher NPGO tends to go with more recruits per spawner. Two things call for caution. With 19 separate intervals, about one in 20 would exclude zero by chance even with no effect at all. And good and bad ocean years affect all stocks at once, so the 19 results are not independent pieces of evidence. Many Stocks fits the stocks together: there, NPGO looks strong until the model also has a shared year effect, and then AIC no longer supports it.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3 (Optional): Check Your Data First (not timed)

    Fit the random-walk model to Early Stuart and find its productivity in the forecast year. Then check the data: which brood years drive that result? Refit without them and compare.

    Plot log(R/S) against brood year, and list the years with the smallest spawner counts (filter(spawners < 1)). You cannot compare the two fits with AIC, because they use different rows: compare the productivity instead.

    R 

    early   <- filter(sockeye, stock == "Early Stuart")
dat_es  <- make_dat(early, S_new = mean(tail(early$spawners, 4)))
walk_es <- fit_model(nll_walk, start_walk(dat_es), dat_es, random = "log_alpha_year")
walk_es$checks
tail(ci_table(walk_es, "random"), 1)         # productivity in the forecast year
early %>%
  mutate(logRS = log(recruits / spawners)) %>%
  filter(spawners < 1)                       # fewer than 1 thousand spawners
early_100  <- filter(early, spawners >= 0.1) # drop the two years with fewer than 100 spawners
dat_es100  <- make_dat(early_100, S_new = mean(tail(early_100$spawners, 4)))
walk_es100 <- fit_model(nll_walk, start_walk(dat_es100), dat_es100, random = "log_alpha_year")
walk_es100$checks
tail(ci_table(walk_es100, "random"), 1)

    OUTPUT 

     finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE
    parameter estimate    lower    upper
75 alpha_year 24.24504 8.454139 69.53067
         stock management_unit brood_year spawners recruits    logRS
1 Early Stuart    Early Stuart       1968    0.795   10.412 2.572372
2 Early Stuart    Early Stuart       2011    0.233    2.366 2.317918
3 Early Stuart    Early Stuart       2019    0.046    0.438 2.253578
4 Early Stuart    Early Stuart       2020    0.015    1.170 4.356709
 finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE
    parameter estimate    lower    upper
75 alpha_year 13.92486 4.103095 47.25746

    The fit passes all four checks and puts productivity in the forecast year at 24 recruits per spawner. But brood years 2019 and 2020 had 46 and 15 spawners (0.046 and 0.015 thousand), and 15 spawners producing 1170 recruits gives the highest log(R/S) in the series, 4.36. The random walk follows the last years, so these two counts raise the forecast productivity by about three quarters: without them it is 14 recruits per spawner instead of 24. The four checks only say that the optimiser found the best values for these data; they cannot say whether the data make sense. Before you trust a model, plot the data, look at the smallest and largest values, ask the people who collected them about anything odd, and report how much the result depends on those years.
